head: Concrete that can't wait,
sent like a taxi.
slides.sub: How Cemex turned chaos into a 20-minute promise.

image.label: A cement mixer truck on a busy Mexican street at dawn
image.brief: 1990년대 멕시코 과달라하라의 새벽 거리를 달리는 레미콘 트럭. 회전하는 드럼, 따뜻한 새벽빛. 실제 회사 로고 없음.

head: A product that
starts to spoil.
body: Ready-mix concrete is mixed at the plant and poured on site. Once mixed, it generally has to be placed within about 90 minutes, or it starts to harden in the drum.
Late trucks mean wasted loads and idle work crews.

image.label: Workers waiting beside an empty foundation
image.brief: 빈 기초 거푸집 옆에서 기다리는 건설 인부들의 실루엣. 시계를 보는 손짓. 1990년대 멕시코 건설 현장.

slides.label: of orders in Guadalajara reportedly changed on the day itself
body: Builders cancelled when it rained, called late when crews weren't ready, or wanted more concrete than planned. Cemex built careful daily schedules, and customers broke them by mid-morning.

image.label: A dispatcher's schedule board covered in crossed-out entries
image.brief: 줄이 그어지고 고쳐 쓴 메모로 가득한 배차 일정판. 전화기와 담배 연기, 1990년대 사무실.

head: The fix made it worse:
a three-hour window.
body: Like the rest of the industry, Cemex asked customers to order ahead and promised delivery within a window that was reportedly about three hours wide.
Crews waited, trucks sat in traffic, and loads were thrown out.

image.label: Mixer trucks stuck in a traffic jam
image.brief: 교통 체증 속에 줄지어 멈춘 레미콘 트럭들. 뜨거운 오후 햇빛, 답답한 분위기.

head: Customers keep changing plans.
What do you do?
body: Your product spoils fast and half your daily plan falls apart. Rivals have the same problem.

options.text: Charge fees for late changes so customers stick to the schedule
options.feedback: It protects your plan, but it pushes the cost of messy job sites onto customers who can't control the weather. Keep swiping.

options.text: Stop planning the day and send trucks as orders come in
options.feedback: This gives up the comfort of a fixed plan and needs tools few cement firms had. Keep swiping.

options.text: Buy more trucks so one is always free
options.feedback: It fixes delays with money. Every extra truck sits idle most of the day. Keep swiping.

image.label: A manager looking at a city map with pins
image.brief: 핀이 꽂힌 도시 지도를 바라보는 관리자의 뒷모습 실루엣. 1990년대 사무실.

head: They studied
ambulances, not cement.
body: In a story often told, Cemex looked at how an emergency dispatch center in Houston and courier FedEx handled unpredictable calls.
Nobody knows when the next emergency comes. Those systems didn't predict it. They stayed ready for it.

image.label: An emergency dispatch room with glowing screens
image.brief: 어두운 응급 배차실, 빛나는 모니터 앞의 일반적인 인물 실루엣들. 1990년대 기술 분위기.

head: Trucks stopped waiting.
They started roaming.
body: In the mid-1990s, Cemex put computers and GPS in its trucks and linked them to its plants. Loaded trucks moved around zones of the city.
When an order came in, the system sent the nearest truck, like a taxi.

image.label: A city map with glowing dots for moving trucks
image.brief: 도시 지도 위에 움직이는 트럭을 나타내는 빛나는 점들과 연결선. 1990년대풍 컴퓨터 화면 그래픽.

slides.label: the new delivery window, reportedly, down from about three hours
body: Cemex reportedly backed the promise with a discount when trucks arrived late. In a business where concrete is concrete, it now sold something rivals couldn't match: certainty.

image.label: A mixer truck arriving as a crew looks up
image.brief: 레미콘 트럭이 현장에 도착하자 인부들이 고개를 드는 장면. 안도감이 느껴지는 밝은 톤.

head: Fewer trucks,
happier customers.
body: Because trucks were used more of the day, Cemex reportedly needed fewer of them for the same work, and fewer loads went to waste.
Reliability let it hold prices better than rivals selling the same gray powder.

image.label: A tidy row of mixer trucks leaving a plant
image.brief: 정돈된 레미콘 공장에서 차례로 출발하는 트럭들. 효율적이고 질서 있는 분위기.

head: Stop fighting the chaos.
Design for it.
body: Everyone defined the problem as customers who wouldn't plan. Cemex redefined it: how do we respond fast when plans change?
That turned a commodity into a service. When the product is the same everywhere, how you deliver it can become the difference.

image.label: Scattered dots forming an orderly pattern
image.brief: 흩어진 점들이 질서 있는 패턴으로 모이는 추상 그래픽.

head: If customers won't change,
change the problem.
body: Forcing customers to be predictable rarely works. Building a business that handles their unpredictability can become your edge.
**Try it today:** list the customer behaviors you complain about most. Which one could you serve better instead of fighting?

image.label: A single mixer truck on an open road at sunset
image.brief: 해 질 녘 텅 빈 도로를 달리는 레미콘 트럭 한 대. 로고 없음.

factChecks.note: 레디믹스 콘크리트는 혼합 후 약 90분 안에 타설해야 한다는 기준(ASTM C94 등 업계 표준)을 확인하세요. 카드에는 "about 90 minutes"로 적었습니다.
과달라하라 고객 주문의 약 절반이 당일 변경·취소되었다는 수치는 Wired(1997) 등 보도 기준입니다. 카드에 "reportedly"로 표시했습니다. 원문 표현을 확인하세요. → [2026-11-02 확인] 과달라하라 주문 절반 당일 변경은 이번 검색에서 미확인.
기존 배송 약속 시간대가 약 3시간이었고 새 시스템 후 약 20분으로 줄었다는 내용은 Wired(1997), HBS 케이스 등 보도 기준입니다. 카드에 "reportedly"로 표시했습니다. → [2026-11-02 확인] 3시간→20분 배송 창은 이번 검색에서 미확인.
Cemex가 휴스턴 911 응급 배차센터와 FedEx 운영을 참고했다는 이야기는 널리 전해지는 이야기로 "a story often told"로 표시했습니다. 출처를 확인하세요.

트럭에 GPS와 컴퓨터를 달아 실시간 배차를 한 시스템(Dynamic Synchronization of Operations)의 도입 시기는 1990년대 중반으로만 적었습니다. 정확한 연도는 HBS 케이스로 확인하세요. → [2026-11-02 확인] 트럭에 컴퓨터·GPS를 달고 중앙 관제와 연결한 Dynamic Synchronization of Operations 확인.
지각 시 할인 보장과 트럭 대수 감소 효과는 보도 기준이며 구체적 금액·비율은 넣지 않았습니다. 카드에는 "reportedly"와 정성 표현만 썼습니다.

sources.text: Katel, P. (1997). Bordering on Chaos. Wired.
Harvard Business School case on CEMEX and its information capabilities (early 2000s)
